title: Consensus, Leader Election and Coordination
summary: Keep one clear owner with Raft, etcd or ZooKeeper. Learn how majorities agree, fencing stops stale owners and logical clocks order events.
body:
Many designs quietly assume that some node is "the" primary, "the" scheduler or "the" holder of a lock. In a distributed system that assumption has to be manufactured: machines pause, networks partition and clocks drift, so two nodes can each believe they are in charge. Consensus is the family of protocols that lets a group of nodes agree on one value, such as who the leader is or what the next log entry is, even when some of them fail. In interviews you rarely implement it. You are expected to know when you need it, to delegate it to a coordination service such as etcd or ZooKeeper, and to protect the rest of the system from the moments when it is uncertain.

## What consensus buys you

For a group of N nodes, a **majority** means floor(N/2) + 1 votes. Three nodes tolerate one failure; five tolerate two. A fourth node still tolerates only one failure while raising the majority from two to three. A communicating majority can make progress once election and message timing allow it; agreement stays safe even when progress pauses. The minority cannot commit new decisions. An isolated old leader may still believe it is in charge, but it cannot form a separate majority and commit conflicting work.

Typical uses:

- **Leader election**: exactly one active scheduler, partition owner or database primary.
- **Configuration and metadata**: which shard lives on which node, feature flags that must be consistent.
- **Membership**: which workers are alive, through sessions or leases that expire.
- **Locks and leases**: mutual exclusion for a job or resource, with an expiry so a dead holder does not block forever.

## Raft at a high level

Raft is the consensus algorithm behind etcd, Consul and CockroachDB's replication; ZooKeeper uses a similar protocol called Zab. Time is divided into numbered **terms**. Each node is a follower, a candidate or the leader. Followers expect a heartbeat from the leader; if none arrives within a randomized election timeout (the Raft paper suggests 150 to 300 ms), a follower increments the term, becomes a candidate and asks for votes. A node grants at most one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. The randomization makes split votes rare.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Node A (follower)
    participant B as Node B
    participant C as Node C
    Note over A: no heartbeat, timeout fires
    A->>B: RequestVote term 5
    A->>C: RequestVote term 5
    B-->>A: vote granted
    Note over A: 2 of 3 votes, A is leader for term 5
    A->>B: AppendEntries: set x=7
    A->>C: AppendEntries: set x=7
    B-->>A: stored
    Note over A: majority stored, entry committed
    A->>B: heartbeat with commit index
    A->>C: heartbeat with commit index
```

A's timeout fires first, so it asks for votes in term 5. Its own vote plus B's gives it two of three votes: a majority, even before C answers. Clients send writes to A, which appends them to its log and replicates them with AppendEntries. In this example, the entry belongs to A's current term. Once a majority has durably stored it, A can mark it **committed**. Raft does not directly commit an older-term entry merely by counting replicas; committing a current-term entry also commits earlier entries in its log. The election's log-up-to-date rule and overlapping majorities together ensure future leaders retain committed entries. Followers apply them in order to the same state machine. If C was partitioned, A backfills its log when it returns.

Consensus costs a round trip to a majority on every write, which is fine for metadata (thousands of writes per second) and wrong for your main data path at millions of writes per second. That is why systems use consensus to choose a leader or assign ranges, then let the leader serve the bulk traffic.

## Quorums without a leader: R + W > N

Dynamo-style stores (Cassandra, Riak, DynamoDB's internals) replicate each key to N nodes and let clients pick how many must acknowledge a write (W) and how many must answer a read (R). If **R + W > N**, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one node, so a read can see the latest acknowledged write. With N = 3, W = 2, R = 2 you tolerate one slow node on either path; W = 1, R = 1 is fast but may return stale data.

| Setting (N = 3) | Read sees latest write? | Availability | Latency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| W = 3, R = 1 | Yes | Writes fail if any replica is down | Slow writes, fast reads |
| W = 2, R = 2 | Yes, if no concurrent writes or sloppy quorum | Tolerates one node down | Balanced |
| W = 1, R = 1 | No guarantee | Highest | Fastest |
| Raft majority | Yes, with leadership confirmation and applied committed state | Needs a majority for quorum-confirmed reads and writes | Client-to-leader trip; quorum confirmation can add a round trip |

Overlap alone is not consensus. Concurrent writes can reach replicas in different orders and need a conflict rule, such as last-writer-wins or version vectors. Sloppy quorums during failures can also break the assumed overlap. Use quorum stores for high-availability data and consensus for decisions that must be unique.

Routing a read to a Raft leader is not enough for **linearizability**: an isolated former leader may still think it owns the job. A quorum-confirmed read, often called ReadIndex, confirms leadership with a majority and waits until the state machine has applied the relevant committed log position before answering. A valid leader-lease optimization can avoid that confirmation on each read only under its clock and timing assumptions. Reading arbitrary local leader state skips those safeguards.

## Coordination services in practice

You should not write Raft. Use **etcd** (Kubernetes' backing store) or **ZooKeeper** (Kafka before KRaft, HBase, many Hadoop systems).

- **Leases and sessions**: etcd attaches keys to a lease with a TTL that the client keeps alive; ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes disappear when the client's session expires. Both give "this key exists only while its owner is alive".
- **Leader election and locks**: create a key with a lease (etcd) or an ephemeral sequential node (ZooKeeper); the lowest sequence or first creator wins, others watch for it to disappear.
- **Watches**: clients subscribe to changes on configuration or membership instead of polling.
- **Compare-and-swap transactions**: etcd's `Txn` updates a key only if its revision matches, the primitive behind safe configuration changes.

Keep the cluster small (3 or 5 nodes), keep data small (etcd's default storage quota is 2 GB), and keep it off the hot request path.

## Leases, fencing and split brain

A lease does not stop a process that does not know it has lost it. A garbage-collection pause, a VM migration or a slow disk can freeze the holder for longer than the TTL. The lock service expires the lease and grants it to a second client; then the first one wakes up and writes, believing it still holds the lock. This is **split brain**, and timeouts cannot prevent it because the paused process cannot observe its own pause.

The fix is a **fencing token**: a number that increases every time the lock is granted (ZooKeeper's zxid or an etcd revision both work). The holder sends the token with every write, and the storage service rejects any token lower than the highest it has seen.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as Lock service
    participant W1 as Worker 1
    participant W2 as Worker 2
    participant S as Storage
    L->>W1: lease granted, token 33
    Note over W1: long GC pause, lease expires
    L->>W2: lease granted, token 34
    W2->>S: write with token 34
    S-->>W2: ok, highest seen = 34
    W1->>S: write with token 33
    S-->>W1: rejected, stale token
```

Worker 1 is paused past its lease, so the lock service hands the lease to Worker 2 with a larger token. Storage accepts token 34 and then rejects Worker 1's late write carrying 33. Fencing requires the protected resource to check tokens; if it cannot (for example a third-party API), design the operation to be idempotent or tolerate a rare duplicate. The same idea protects database failover: a demoted primary must be fenced (shut down, or its storage access revoked) before the new one accepts writes.

## Clocks cannot order events

It is tempting to resolve conflicts with timestamps. Wall clocks on different machines drift and are corrected by NTP, typically to within milliseconds but sometimes much worse, and they can jump backward. A write at 10:00:00.005 on node A may really have happened after a write stamped 10:00:00.010 on node B, so last-writer-wins by wall clock silently discards data. Use a monotonic clock for measuring durations, never the wall clock.

To order events, use **logical clocks**. A Lamport clock is a counter incremented on each event and advanced past any timestamp received, which gives an order consistent with causality. Vector clocks additionally detect concurrent updates. **Hybrid logical clocks** combine physical time with a logical counter so timestamps stay close to real time while respecting causality; CockroachDB uses them. Google Spanner takes another route: TrueTime exposes clock uncertainty explicitly and transactions wait out that uncertainty before committing.

## Common interview mistakes

- "Use a Redis lock" for correctness-critical work without fencing or idempotency.
- Even-sized consensus clusters, or a single coordinator node.
- Putting consensus on every user request.
- Treating R + W > N as full linearizability.
- Ordering events across machines by wall-clock timestamps.

## How to use it in an interview

When the design needs a single owner, say so explicitly: "One scheduler instance holds a lease in etcd; others are on standby. Jobs carry the lease's fencing token and the job table rejects stale tokens." State the failure tolerance (5 nodes, survives 2), the failover time (election timeout plus lease TTL, typically seconds), and what happens during it (writes pause, reads may continue from followers if staleness is acceptable). Expect follow-ups on network partitions, paused leaders and how clients discover the new leader.

## Interview exercise

A cron service runs 10,000 scheduled jobs per hour across 20 workers, and no job may run twice concurrently. Design leader election or per-job locking with etcd, specify lease TTLs and fencing, and walk through what happens when the worker running a billing job pauses for 40 seconds and then resumes.

## Further reading

- [The Raft consensus algorithm](https://raft.github.io/) links to the paper and a visualization.
- [etcd documentation](https://etcd.io/docs/) covers leases, watches and transactions.
- [Apache ZooKeeper documentation](https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/current/) includes recipes for locks and leader election.
keyTakeaways: Consensus needs a majority, so 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure and 5 tolerate 2; the minority side cannot make progress.
Raft commits current-term entries after durable majority replication; older entries commit with them. Linearizable reads also need confirmed leadership and applied committed state.
R + W > N makes read and write sets overlap but does not by itself resolve concurrent writes.
Leases expire while a paused holder still acts; fencing tokens checked by the resource prevent split brain.
Wall clocks cannot order events across machines; use logical or hybrid logical clocks.
